en: *Fanggui*, Scroll Five, Part Two, composed by the Śramaṇa Zhiyan of Zhixiang Monastery on Mount Zhongnan.
From this point forward are ten spiritual friends; this [first] one is a Bodhisattva of the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).
The goddess is named Vāsavadattā; she has entered the Dharma-door of "Universal Radiance Entering All Dharmas to Shatter and Dispel the Ignorance of Sentient Beings.

This is divided into three parts: first, the preliminary exposition of the exhortation; second, from "At that time, Sudhana... onwards, the entry based upon [the teaching]; and third, from "Then the Night Goddess said... onwards, the clarification of entering the Dharma-realm.
The three [stages] within the "Exhortation and Instruction" are as previously described.
To this is added the city of Kapilavastu; the kingdom is named Śākya, which is the Buddha’s birthplace, signifying birth into the family of the Tathāgata at the first stage (bhūmi).

Therefore, from this point onward, all [deities] are night-goddesses (*rātridevatā*), intended to manifest the attainment of mastery over principles hereafter; they illuminate the vast expanse of the great night by transforming it into deep darkness.
The rest has already been clarified previously.
Second, regarding the entry [into the intermediate state], there are seven parts: first, departing;
second, recollecting the previous dharma-gate; and so forth.
Third, the place of arrival;
fourth, from "From the eastern gate" downward, there is the gradual approach and seeking, which can be understood as having two parts;
fifth, from "Seeing him" downward, there are the signs of seeing, which have two parts: first, the act of seeing, and second, observing his virtues.
6. From "Having seen and heard this" onwards, it clarifies the joy of prostration;
7. The spontaneous declaration of generating the resolve and the inquiry, which may be understood through three phrases.
As for the eastern gate, it is the beginning of opening and clarifying.
Third, from "He said" onwards is the actual entry into the middle [section], which consists of three major parts:

first, praising the arousal of the mind and following the instructions of the spiritual friend; second, from "I have already accomplished" onwards, explaining the dharma-gate of one's own level; and third, from "The great ones" onwards, looking up to and extolling the superior levels.
The intermediate state (*antarābhava*) consists of four parts:

first, the identification of the name and essence of the dharma; second, the analysis of its function, beginning with "I [regarding] good and evil"; third, the clarification of the causes and conditions for attaining the dharma, beginning with "He spoke, saying..."; and fourth, the summary of what is personally known, beginning with "I alone..."
There are three parts to this section:

first, the arousal of compassion and skillful means toward sentient beings; second, from "I am always thus" onwards, the transformation of others in accordance with conditions based on the aforementioned skillful means; and third, the recitation of verses to exhort practice.
The second section, concerning the transformation of those in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), consists of seventeen passages:

first, a general response; second, rescuing from the perils of the sea; third, rescuing from land-based perils; fourth, acting as a refuge; fifth, rescuing from mountain perils; sixth, rescuing from wilderness perils; seventh, rescuing from perils of suffering; eighth, rescuing from attachment to lands; ninth, rescuing from attachment to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*); tenth, rescuing from attachment to villages; eleventh, rescuing from attachment to the six sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*); twelfth, rescuing from delusion; thirteenth, rescuing from evil karma; fourteenth, rescuing from calamities; fifteenth, rescuing from the three obstacles such as suffering; sixteenth, rescuing from the three types of erroneous karma; and seventeenth, the inclusion within the practices of Samantabhadra.
Within these three verses, there are two parts:
first, the prose section that precedes the verses, and second, the verse section itself.
The verses consist of twenty-one stanzas.

The first verse explains the preceding dharma-gate; the next four verses exhort one to bring to completion the four immeasurable practices upon first entering the stage; the subsequent thirteen stanzas exhort the cultivation of completion regarding the superior functions of the six sense-bases; and the final three stanzas offer a general praise for the superior functions of the dharma-gates thus attained.

Among the preceding thirteen verses: the first [verse] concerns the dharma-body and so forth, which is the supernormal power of recollecting past lives; "my mind" and so forth constitute two verses on the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others; "I, by means of my spiritual power" and so forth constitute two verses on the supernormal power of the body; and the single verse on "pure and vast wisdom" concerns the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows.
Within the third section on the causes and conditions for attaining the Dharma, there is first the question and then the answer.
In the question, first is the inquiry regarding the duration of the kalpa when the resolve was made, and second is the inquiry regarding the length of time since attaining this Dharma-gate.
The answers to the two preceding questions each have their respective concluding passages, which may be understood from the text.
In the "Respectful Deduction" section, there is first an extensive exposition, followed by a conclusion.

On the second night, the name of the night goddess was Profound and Wondrous Virtue Free from Defilement Radiance; she represents the stage of a Bodhisattva on the second ground (*dvitīyā bhūmiḥ*), having entered the Bodhisattva’s dharma-gate of the joy of the samādhi of quiescence and diligent application.
First, there are three aspects of the initial exhortation and instruction, which may be understood;
second, from "At that time, Sudhana... onwards is the entry based upon [the instruction];
third, from "He replied... onwards is the actual entry.
Second, regarding the entry [into the womb], there are seven parts:

first, ten verses praising the virtues of the aforementioned knowledge; within these ten verses, the first six praise the virtues of the *saṃbhogakāya*, the next one praises how the practices of the fundamental cause manifest within the body, and the final three praise the inexhaustible utility [of the Buddha];
second, taking leave to depart.
Third, the three types of mindfulness, within which two aspects may be discerned;
fourth, gradual arrival; fifth, reaching [the destination].
Sixth, paying respect;
seventh, the spontaneous declaration of the resolve for enlightenment and the inquiry.
Within the third section, "The Actual Entry," there are three major divisions:

First, the praise of the arousal of the mind; second, from "The bodhisattva accomplishes ten dharmas" onwards, the elucidation of the dharma-gate of self-perfection (*svabhāga*); third, from "All the great [bodhisattvas]" onwards, the reverent recommendation.
The second [section], "One's Own," has three parts.
First, the analysis of the essential nature and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) has two sub-sections.

First, the analysis of the essential nature and characteristics; this passage contains four points as can be known. Within these thirty gates, the first four concern self-benefit (*svārtha*), and the subsequent six concern the benefit of others (*parārtha*).
Second, from "I have already" onwards, the names are concluded.
Second, from "All see" onwards, the great function is clarified; this passage has four parts:
first, a general exposition of the characteristics of the function.

2. From "Nor is there attachment" onwards, the substance of the practice is established through its application; this consists of four parts—namely, the proposition, the objection, the response, and the concluding response—which may be understood accordingly.
3. From "Discerning and fully knowing" onwards, it clarifies that the two applications function in tandem.
4. From "I am thus" onwards, the characteristics of the application are extensively analyzed; other characteristics may be understood as follows.
The third section, beginning with "I alone," can be understood as the conclusion.
Within the section on looking upward in reliance [on others], there is first a detailed explanation and subsequently a summary.

Regarding the third night goddess named *Nayanānanda* (Joyful Eyes), she is a Bodhisattva of the third stage who has entered the Dharma-gate of the Banner of Joy Free from Defilement (*Vimalānandadhvaja*).
First, the exhortation; second, from "At that time, Sudhana" onwards, entering according to the instruction; third, from "He saw that Night Goddess" onwards, the actual entry.
Within the instruction, there are four parts:
first, indicating the location; second, indicating the person; third, instructing him to go and inquire; fourth, from "At that time, Profound" onwards, exhorting him to visit by means of verses.
In the verses, the first twelve summarize the ten preceding dharmas; the next one instructs Sudhana to visit his subsequent spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Within the former section, the first two verses summarize the first four dharmas, while the following ten verses summarize the latter six dharmas.
Regarding the second [section], entering [the state] based on the two [conditions], there are four parts:
first, departing with words;
second, recollecting the person before one and employing the Dharma through the ear.
The Deva Priyadarśana of the Three Times bestows his grace upon Sudhana to cause him to proceed; this is for the purpose of praising the spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). This section has two parts:
first, the praise; second, the attainment of the dharma-gate.
The first part itself contains two sub-sections, which may be understood accordingly.
4. "Sudhana goes" and below is the actual journey.
Within the third section, "The actual entry," there are two parts:
first, the exposition of the dharma-gate of one's own stage; second, from "All the great [beings]" onwards, the reverent inference.
The preceding text consists of four parts:

first, the elucidation of the essence of the Dharma; second, from "All pores" onwards, the discernment of the great function of the Dharma-gate; third, from "He said" onwards, the causes and conditions for attaining the Dharma; and fourth, from "I only" onwards, the conclusion regarding his own name.
Within the Great Function, there are two parts:
first, the manifestation of virtues; second, from "At that time, Sudhana was able to see and hear" onwards, the attainment of benefits.
The first section has three parts:
The analysis of the virtues of practicing the ten perfections in the present has two parts:
a brief explanation, followed by a summary that indicates the extensive classification; these may be understood accordingly.
Second, from "Joyful Eyes" (*Nayanānanda*) onwards, the virtues of his past practices are clarified; this has three parts: namely, the general statement, the explanation, and the conclusion.
Third, from "Body Clouds" (*Kāyamegha*) onwards, the manifestation of the body for the sake of gathering and benefiting beings is presented; this text has four sections:
first, the manifestation of the body, which has three parts—namely, the general statement, the explanation, and the conclusion.
Second, from "for the sake of all sentient beings" onwards, the qualities manifested are explained;
third, from "such as these" onwards, the sounds of the verbal teachings that express them are explained;
fourth, from "when each of those clouds of bodies speaks this Dharma" onwards, the benefits obtained through the teaching are explained.
Furthermore, these correspond respectively to the first [category], the body; the next, the mind; and the third, the three types of bodily action (*kāyakarman*).

Within the first ten clouds of the body, each possesses four meanings: namely, (1) the basis, (2) the body itself, (3) the activity performed, and (4) the benefit conferred; these may be understood accordingly.
Regarding the second, the past practices, the *upāya-pāramitā* (perfection of skillful means) consists of five points:

first, the essence of the initial practice; second, the skillful manifestation of the environment and its inhabitants (*bhājanaloka* and *sattvaloka*) according to circumstances; third, the functional activity of that which is known; fourth, sovereign unimpededness; and fifth, the objective basis upon which skillful means relies.
The vow has five phrases, which may be understood by analogy with the *upāya* (expedient means).
Power has four phrases:
first, the essence of practice;
Second, the virtue of being the causal condition for the accomplishment of all phenomena;
third, the ocean of skillfulness regarding the Dharma;
fourth, the thirty phrases within the wisdom of the objective basis, wherein the first is the essence and the second is the manifestation of characteristics that establishes the teaching.
1. Meaning; 2. The basis for the three knowledges; 3. The characteristics of the eloquence of the four knowledges;
4. The fivefold limits; 5. The sixfold inclusion of types; 6. The superior capacities of the seven knowledges; 7. The objective bases; 8. The distinctions; 9.
The ultimate source to be fathomed; 10. Grasping according to function; 11. Non-contradiction with the rules of conduct; 12. Wisdom.
14. The causal factors; 15. The knowledge of the time of the dependent retribution (*niśraya-vipāka*); 16. The knowledge of the time of the primary retribution (*pratyaya-vipāka*);
17. The manifestation of the person who has attained the fruit; 18. The knowledge of the wisdom of the person who has attained the fruit;

19. The knowledge of the person on the path of cause; 20. The knowledge of the wisdom of the person on the path of cause; 21. The knowledge that knows the stage of the person on the path of cause; 2. [Continuation of the list].
21. Merit based on persons; 22. Transformation based on persons; 23. Ability to support vows and practices;
24. Bestowing the limits of practice; 25. Knowing the limits of teaching; 26. Dharma-Indra; 27.
Fellow practitioners of the Dharma; 28. Knowledge of the Dharma that accords with the Path.
30. Knowing the destination.
Second, Sudhana’s attainment of benefit, which has two parts:
first, the attainment of benefit; second, the praise in verse.
The initial passage consists of four parts, which may be understood as follows.

Within the ten verses, the first seven praise the transformative function of the body-karma of the spiritual friend; the next one praises the transformative function of his mental karma; the next one praises the transformative function of his verbal karma; and the final one collectively praises the vastness of these transformative functions.
Within the causes and conditions for attaining the Dharma, there are three parts:

first, the conclusion of the preceding section and the introduction of the subsequent inquiry; second, the night goddess’s response with eighty-nine and a half verses; third, the synthesis of the ancient and the present.

In the response, the first twenty-five points answer the duration and proximity of the initial arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*); the subsequent sixty-four and a half points answer the causes and conditions for attaining the Dharma.
Within the section on "looking up to [the Buddha]," there is first a detailed explanation and secondly a summary.

The fourth night goddess is named Wondrous Virtue Who Protects and Rescues Sentient Beings; she corresponds to the stage of a Bodhisattva of the Fourth Ground and enters the Bodhisattva Dharma-gate of Teaching and Transforming Sentient Beings.

First, the exhortation and instruction; second, from "At that time, Sudhana... onwards, entering according to the instruction; third, from "At that time, the Night Goddess... onwards, the realization.
Within the first section on the exhortation and instruction, there are three parts, as before.
Second, regarding the entry [into the intermediate state], there are three parts:
verbal recollection, the prior dharma, and going to see; these are abbreviated as they lack the formal greetings and inquiries.
Third, regarding the actual entry, there are two parts:
First is the explanation of one's own attainment; second, from "All the Great Bodhisattvas" onwards, is the reverent inference.
Within the first section on one's own attainment, there are four parts:

first, the manifestation of the Dharma-gate by the deva to enable Sudhana to attain the essence of his own attainment; second, from "Immediately he attained this samādhi" onwards, clarifying the power and function of the samādhi; third, from "He addressed [the deva]" onwards, clarifying the causes and conditions for attaining the Dharma.
4. From "I alone" below, the conclusion of what is known by oneself is presented.
This section has four parts:
first, distinguishing the dharma-gate of the bodhisattva as the basis; second, manifesting the body and light; third, distinguishing the destination; and fourth, obtaining benefits.
Regarding the power and function of the two samādhis, there are three sections in the text.
First, explaining the sovereign mastery over the realms of the sentient beings to be transformed; herein there are four parts:
first, the basis;...
There are four points: second, the two locations; third, knowledge;
fourth, benefit. Within this passage, there are these four:

First, the six destinies; second, the four modes of birth; third, the analysis according to characteristics; fourth, from "fulfilling the great vows" onwards, the explanation that establishes the intent of transformation.
Second, from "Sudhana saw him" onwards, Sudhana attains benefit and gives rise to reverence.

3. From "He immediately relinquished his marks and signs" (*lakṣaṇavyañjana*) onwards, the purpose of the teaching is exhausted; this serves to induce movement in the practitioner's mind and causes Sudhana to offer praise in verse.
This consists of two parts: the prose narrative and the verses.
This verse-text consists of twenty and a half verses and has three parts:

first, ten and a half verses briefly praise the sovereign power of the Night Goddess’s transformative activity; second, the three verses beginning with "Joyful Eyes" praise the causes and conditions for being able to see her; and third, seven verses extensively praise how the Night Goddess transforms all sentient beings and brings them to fulfillment in their supreme practices.
Regarding the causes and conditions for attaining the Dharma, there are two parts:
first, Sudhana briefly praises the dharma-gate and poses three questions;

second, from "Good son" onwards, the celestial deity provides a detailed answer. Within this answer, the first part praises the profundity of the Dharma, while the second part—from "Listen attentively" onwards—properly answers the causes and conditions for attaining the Dharma as well as the duration of the kalpas, which is the answer found within the fourth section of the conclusion.
The initial section has three parts:
first, a general praise;
second, from "All humans and devas" onwards, [it shows that this] is not the realm of those with small minds; third, [the section on] the Bodhisattvas.
Third, from "Why is this? onwards is the explanation and establishment [of the argument], which can be understood to have two parts.
The direct answer has two sections:
first, the prose (gadya), and second, the verse (śloka).
The prose section has two parts:
first, the admonition for the assembly to listen; second, the exposition.
Within the exposition, there are two further sections.
First, one encounters a Buddha and hears the True Dharma;
second, from the passage "After that kalpa" onwards, five hundred Buddhas appear in the world, and [the practitioner] goes to make offerings to them in various forms. This section has two parts:
first, the explanation, and second, the conclusion regarding the benefits.
The first section concerns the initial encounter with a Buddha, which contains eight parts:
first, the appearance of a Buddha during that particular kalpa;
second, from "At that time, in that city," onwards, it clarifies the king to whom [the Buddha] belonged.
3. From "She had a daughter" onwards, it clarifies the practice of her own body;
4. From "At that time, to the north of the city" onwards, it clarifies the Buddha’s manifestation of transformation;
5. From "Then the woman immediately understood" onwards, it clarifies the initial conditions for receiving transformation and attaining benefit.
Six: From "At that time, Subhūti... among the great assembly" onwards, the text correctly clarifies the attainment of benefits, which has four parts:

first, the Buddha’s preaching of the sutra; second, the girl’s attainment of meditative concentration; third, her attainment of a superior mind; and fourth, her acquisition of a supreme dharma-gate. Seven:
From "Furthermore, prior to this" onwards, there is a further explanation of the past causal origin.
8. From "At that time, King Vimalaprabha and others" onwards, the connection between the past and the present is concluded; four points can be discerned therein.
Regarding the fourfold manifestation of transformation, there are two sections in the text:

first, the Buddha’s universal manifestation and preaching of the Dharma; second, from "At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva" onwards, the specific instruction for those who are ready to receive it.
Within the initial passage there are four sections:
first, the description of the adornments of the Bodhi tree;

second, the original Buddha’s attainment of enlightenment and the emission of twelve kinds of light to nourish the faculties of sentient beings, which correspond to the twelve stages of abiding (*dvādaśa-vihāra*).

3. From "When the seven days were complete" onwards, there are three points: knowing the time for receiving the Way; the shaking of the earth and the sounding of voices; and turning the Wheel of Dharma according to the capacities of those who are suitable vessels.
4. From "For what reason? onwards is the explanation that establishes these points.

Within the Turning of the Wheel of Dharma, there are twenty phrases: the first two benefit ordinary persons (*bālapṛthagjana*) and others; the next one benefits those of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*); the next ten benefit those of the Ten Faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*); the section beginning with "establishing the immeasurable" benefits those of the Ten Understandings (*daśa-adhimukti*); the section beginning with "establishing the dwelling of the immeasurable bodhisattva" benefits those of the Ten Practices (*daśa-caryā*); the section beginning with "immeasurable purity" benefits those of the Dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), causing them to enter the First Ground (*prathamā bhūmi*); [the sections] from the Seventh through the Ninth cause one to enter the Tenth Ground (*daśamī bhūmi*); the section beginning with "having established immeasurable sentient beings" causes those of the Tenth Ground to enter the ultimate stage of the Abiding Portion (*anusthāna-bhāga*); and the Tenth accomplishes the stage of Samantabhadra’s practice (*samantabhadracaryā-vihāra*).
Second, the responsive capacity of the audience, which has three parts:
first, Samantabhadra’s observation of the capacity; second, the king, his attendants, and others knowing [the teaching] and formally addressing it with verses; third, the presentation of offerings.
Within the "Ten Verses of Praise by the Holy King" (*Daśastava*), there are two parts:
first, the prose introduction; second, the verses.

Within the verses, the first praises the Buddha and exhorts the assembly to go to him; the next six praise the difficulty of encountering him; the following two demonstrate the light to inspire joy; and the final one exhorts people to go quickly.
Within the second section, the *Gāthā* (Verses), there are two parts:
first, the prose introduction, and second, the verses.
The verse text consists of thirty-eight and a half [units] and contains four sections:
The first two [verses] are the imperial decree permitting the exposition;
the next thirty-three and a half [verses] briefly clarify the one hundred and ten Buddhas, summarizing the Buddhas of the aforementioned dust-motes and so forth;
the final two [verses] concern the Dharma-gates attained by the Buddhas.
The following section encourages Sudhana to swiftly cultivate and fulfill [the practices].
Within the exhortation, there is first an explanation and then a conclusion.
The fifth night goddess is named Śāntamati; she represents the stage of a Bodhisattva on the fifth bhūmi and has entered the Dharma-gate of the Adornment of Immeasurable Joy.

First, the exhortation and instruction; second, from "At that time, Sudhana" onwards, entering according to the instruction; third, from "The Night Goddess said" onwards, the actual entry into the Dharma-realm.
Within the section on the instruction, there are three parts, which are the same as before.
Second, regarding the entry [into the assembly], there are only four parts:
first, taking leave; second, going; third, prostrating; and fourth, walking upon the ground and inquiring.
Third, regarding the actual entry, there are three parts:

First, the praise of the arousal of the mind; second, from "I have accomplished" onwards, the teaching of the dharma-gate of one's own portion (*svabhāga*); third, from "The great bodhisattvas" onwards, the reverent inference of the superior portion (*viśeṣabhāga*).
This section on one's own realization (*sva-adhigama*) consists of four parts:

first, the identification of the essence of the dharma-gate; second, from "He said" (*āha*) onwards, the clarification of the merit and function of the dharma-gate; third, from "He said to the deva" (*āha deva*) onwards, the causes and conditions for attaining the dharma; and fourth, from "I only... (*ahaṃ kevalam*) onwards, the summary of what one has realized.
Within the section on the function of virtue, there is first the question and then the answer.
The question consists of four points:

first, the inquiry regarding the virtuous function of gathering and transforming; second, the inquiry regarding the distinctions in the essence, characteristics, and boundaries of the dharma-gates and their spheres; third, the inquiry regarding the skillful means of cultivation and practice; and fourth, the inquiry regarding correct practice itself.
The response can be understood through its four parts.
The first section contains three sub-divisions:

first, the explanation of meditative cultivation; second, the formal explanation of gathering and transforming beings, beginning with "I act for... and so forth; and third, the concluding summary, beginning with "Good son... and so forth.
The first section contains nine points concerning the mind, which may be understood as they appear.

The second section, "Correctly Gathering and Transforming Beings," has five parts: first, generally causing sentient beings suffering to leave that suffering; second, from "If he sees those living at home" onwards, transforming them through the gates of the ten perfections and so forth; third, from "The formless realm" onwards, transforming those attached to their primary retribution (*sabhāga-niṣyanda*); fourth, from "For gardens and pavilions" onwards, transforming those attached to their secondary environment (*adhiṣṭhāna-vipāka*); fifth, from "For those with greed and desire" onwards, gathering them through the gates of the five perfections to cultivate superior practices.

Among the three fetters (*saṃyojana*), the first fetter consists of: the first phrase, which is a general announcement; the second phrase, which binds the attachment to the environment and its inhabitants (*āśraya-adhiṣṭhāna*); and the third phrase, which binds the gates such as the ten perfections (*pāramitā*).
Furthermore, it may also be understood that there are only three intended meanings that collectively conclude the preceding text.
The text consists of two parts: first, the general overview; second, the detailed exposition.
Second, the response to the preceding question regarding the objective realm (*viṣaya*) has four sections:
first, the analysis of the object of contemplation as practiced through causal cultivation;
2. From "Furthermore, good son" onwards, it clarifies the objective realm perceived by the virtues of the fruit;
3. From "Arising is not... onwards, there are three points to be known regarding the sublation of appearances to enter into reality;
4. From "O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva" onwards, it is the conclusion.
Third, the response regarding the preparatory application for cultivation consists of three parts:
first, a general summary; second, the specific details; and third, the conclusion, which may be understood accordingly.
Within the specific details, there are thirty-one phrases, which may likewise be understood.
Regarding the fourth [section], the response concerning correct practice (*samyak-pratipatti*), there are two parts:
first, the question; second, the answer.
The answer consists of five points, which may be understood accordingly.
Regarding the duration of the initial arousal of the bodhicitta among the three types of illumination, there is first the question and then the answer.
Within the answer, there is first the prose and then the verse.
The prose section contains six parts:

1. First, the Buddha’s attainment of the Dharma; 2. From "In that place of enlightenment" downward, by the power of the Dharma, he constantly beholds all Buddhas; 3. From "Passing through Buddha-fields" downward, again by the power of the Dharma, he beholds the four Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa; 4. From "By means of this dharma-realm" downward, he further attains immeasurable dharma-gates; 5. From "That which you have asked me" downward, he concludes by reconciling the vast and true nature that is without increase or decrease; 6. From "Therefore" downward, he exhorts [the audience] to practice.
The second verse-verse section has two parts:
first, the introductory prose;
second, the actual verses, which consist of ten [units] divided into three sections:

The first verse is an imperial decree permitting and encouraging cultivation; the next four verses explain the causes and conditions for the Dharma-gates attained above; and the final five verses clarify the meaning of benefiting sentient beings through the accomplishment of superior practice.
Looking upward to extol Wen, there is first the separation and next the conclusion.

On the sixth night, the deity was named Wondrous Virtue Guardian of All Cities; this corresponds to the stage of a Bodhisattva of the sixth ground, who has entered the Dharma-gate of the Profoundly Sublime and Sovereign Sound of Virtue.

First, the exhortation to enter; second, from "At that time, Sudhana" onwards, the approach according to the instruction; third, from "The Night Goddess said" onwards, the actual entry into the Dharma-realm.
The first section has three parts, as before.
Second, regarding the entry [into the city], there are seven sections.
First, as Sudhana was about to depart, he first offered praise and expressed his gratitude in verse; within these ten verses, there are two [parts]:

First, the initial arising; second, the verses. Within the verses: the first three praise how, by virtue of the teaching, one is free from all grasping and attains the vision of the Dharmakāya; the next two praise how the Bodhisattvas, being free from the three obstacles, attain liberation and mastery; the next three praise the Bodhisattvas' gathering and benefiting of others; and the final two cause the assembly of that time to be free from grasping.
Second, the formal salutation and departure; third, the recollection of the preceding Dharma-gate.
Fourth, approaching;
fifth, seeing the superior marks;
sixth, paying respectful homage.
The seven questions.
Regarding the three aspects of the correct entry into the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), there are three parts:

first, praising the ability to ask such questions regarding the arousal of the mind; second, from "I have already... onwards, explaining what has been attained by oneself; third, from "All the Great... onwards, looking up to and extolling the superior qualities [of others].

This section consists of four parts: first, the identification of the essence of the dharma-gate; second, the clarification of the function of the dharma, beginning with "Therefore, O Son of the Buddha, for my sake..."; third, the causes and conditions regarding the duration of attaining the dharma, beginning with "He addressed the Night Goddess..."; and fourth, the conclusion of what is known within this specific category, beginning with "I only... and so forth.
Within the application of these two dharma-gates, there are four sections.
First, the twenty-three phrases clarify the skillful means for contemplative cultivation and the gathering of beings through transformation;

this has three parts: first, one phrase establishes the premise; second, the section beginning with "Regarding all dharmas" provides the explanation; third, the section beginning with "O Sons of the Buddha, we... provides the conclusion.
The second passage has four parts:

first, based on the Dharma; second, based on the world; third, from "equal mind" downward, based on sentient beings; and fourth, from "O Son of the Buddha, I always... downward, establishing the function of the virtues of the mind.

first, the statement that in reality there is no coming; second, from "It is only for the sake of teaching and transforming" onwards, the discussion of the location as existing through the gathering of conditions; and third, from "Regarding what you asked me" onwards, the manifestation of the direction from which he emerged in order to attract sentient beings.
Regarding the second question on the place of birth, there are two parts:
first, distinguishing the causal practice, essence, and place of birth; second, from "I, in this Jambudvīpa" onwards, clarifying the place where the transformation body manifests its coming birth.
The initial text has five parts:
first, the identification of the place of birth;
second, from "taking Prajñā as mother" onwards, nineteen phrases that specifically clarify the practices of the retinue.
3. From "Transcending the Stage of Ordinary Beings" (*pṛthagjanabhūmi*) below, there is a comparative evaluation of superiority and inferiority;
4. From "Born into such a family" below, ten phrases distinguish the excellence of the stage;
5. From "My pure Dharma-body" (*dharmakāya*) below, ten phrases distinguish the correspondence between the retribution and the essence, which is the excellence of the essence itself.

Regarding the second point, the birthplaces of the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) are divided into three categories: first, among humans; second, in the heavens; and third, being born again among humans—each of these being his final birth.

The fourth wisdom illuminates the non-dual aspect; this person is named Mañjuśrī. It is the Dharma-gate of entering the universal vision that accords with the teachings of spiritual friends, also known as the Bodhisattva’s Dharma-gate of Quiescence.
The text consists of three parts:

first, from "Good son, go to Mañjuśrī" onwards, which explains the exhortation to advance; second, from "Then Sudhana" onwards, which describes the selection according to the instructions and the actual entry; third, from "At that time, Sudhana" onwards, which is the formal entry into the Dharma-realm.
The initial passage consists of three parts:
first, the indication of the person's name; second, the presentation of the inquiry regarding the teaching; and third, from "For what reason" onwards, the praise of his virtues.
Herein, the location is omitted briefly, as it is stated in the subsequent text: "He arrived at the country of Samantamukha."
There are six aspects to the praise of virtues:
first, the inquiry;
second, the response, which constitutes the praise of virtues itself.
3. From "Good son" onwards, it is shown again by way of exhortation;
4. From "Therefore" onwards, it is the conclusion of the exhortation;
5. The repeated reprimand.
Sixth is the answer.

Within the process of entering according to the teaching, there are four parts: first, the respectful salutation; second, the taking leave; third, traveling through one hundred and ten cities to gradually reach the destination; and fourth, the selection.
The Land of Universal Gates is a place where Mañjuśrī briefly manifests his transformation; it may also be understood as the "Universal Dharma" that serves as the basis for wisdom.
Within the third section, the actual entry [into realization], there are two parts:
first, the vision, and second, the attainment of benefit.
Therefore, it does not say "preaching the Dharma," because it realizes that there is no verbal expression.
Therefore, the universal vision herein is intended to signify that great wisdom universally illuminates non-duality.
The reason for not mentioning seeing Mañjuśrī is to manifest that universal illumination is free from the characteristics of seeing.
Not contradicting his teaching means being in accord with the various spiritual friends through the patience of compliance.
Regarding "the two increases" and so forth: the realization and benefit reside within oneself.

Herein there are four parts: first, accomplishing the benefit of others; second, from "abiding" onwards, accomplishing one's own practice; third, from "entering the profoundness of the Buddha" onwards, conforming to the superior portion; and fourth, from "manifestly entering the various realms of existence" onwards, clarifying that the virtues of self and others are accomplished through entry into the conduct of Samantabhadra.
Below this, the fifth section reveals the characteristics of the vastness of the cause. The person is named Samantabhadra, who enters the dharma-gate of the ten indestructible wisdoms.
This has three parts:
first, regarding Sudhana hearing the name of Samantabhadra, there is the instruction and exhortation to advance further.
2. From "With a single mind, he desired to see Samantabhadra" onwards, there is the entry according to the teaching;
3. From "Sudhana then saw Samantabhadra" onwards, there is the actual realization of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
The initial passage has two parts:
first, hearing the name of Samantabhadra, which indicates his name;
second, from "Vows and Practices" onwards, which praises his virtues.
The meaning of these expressions such as "no place of indication" can be understood through reflection.
Regarding the phrase "hearing the name of Samantabhadra," one should understand that it refers to hearing the four types of "universality" (*pūrvokta*) mentioned above:

first, within the scriptural authority (*āgama*), Mañjuśrī is fully endowed with the practices of Samantabhadra; second, within the process of entering [the path], he reaches the land of Universal Gate (*Samantamukha*); third, within direct realization (*sākṣātkriyā*), he universally beholds all spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*); and fourth, after realization, he cultivates the practices of Samantabhadra through subsequent knowledge (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*). Therefore, it is said that he "hears" [them].
The text for praising these virtues consists of eleven phrases:
the first, "the practices, vows, and stages," is general; the subsequent ten phrases are specific.

Within the general section, the first reveals the practice of aspiration and joy prior to the stages (*bhūmi*), while the second praises the merit of the foundational positions attained upon entering the stages.
Within the distinctions, "the ground being complete" refers to the practice that constitutes the cause for attaining the grounds.
"The dharmas of the ground" refers to the ten dharma-realms, as these constitute the essence of the ground.
"Attaining the ground" means internalizing them within oneself through realization.
"Successive" refers to the beginning and end of each stage (*bhūmi*).
"Cultivation of the stages" refers to the fourfold and fivefold cultivations, and so forth.
"Abiding" refers to the completion of cultivation within that particular stage.

Regarding the "stages" (*bhūmi*) and their "objects" (*viṣaya*): the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) and the three non-natures (*triniḥsvabhāvatā*) may also be categorized by division; these are the objects of focus for the stages. Regarding "sustaining" (*dhāraṇa*):
it means that the object sustains the contemplative mind; it may also mean that the cause sustains the fruit.
The "shared" refers to the ten practices such as faith, compassion, loving-kindness, and equanimity, which collectively bring all the stages (*bhūmi*) to fruition.
The "correct path" is fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).
Regarding the two modes of entry, there are two [types]:
The first line initiates the correct aspiration; the second section, beginning with "the realm of space," etc., explains the skillful means for entering [the path].
This passage has two parts:
first, Sudhana’s general contemplation of the pure land and the dharmakāya; second, the manifestation of auspicious signs beginning from the phrase "when this mind arose."
This passage consists of three parts:

first, the analysis of the causes and conditions for seeing; second, from "that very seeing" onwards, the actual characteristics of seeing; and third, the conclusion of the preceding and the introduction of what follows.
Within the section on the manifestation of signs, there are two parts:
The first ten [verses] reveal the characteristics of the pure land; the subsequent ten reveal the characteristics of the Dharma-body.

Furthermore, it may also be said that the first ten manifest the pure realm of the land and the pure world of sentient beings, while the subsequent ten manifest the pure Indra-net realm and the limits of the perfection of wisdom and awakening—intending thereby to clarify the scope of Samantabhadra.

The threefold entry into realization consists of five parts: first, the elucidation of Samantabhadra’s virtues and activities in terms of his gathering and transforming of beings; second, the section beginning with “I, in the past,” which reiterates Samantabhadra’s original causes and exhorts the practice of supreme conduct; third, the section beginning with “Sudhana’s journey through proximity,” which compares and reveals his excellence; fourth, the section beginning with “Sudhana was able to bring himself to ultimate fulfillment,” which praises the excellence of Sudhana’s practice; and fifth, the concluding verses in praise of the Buddha that bring the work to its close.
The initial text has four parts:
first, a general vision of all Tathāgatas, such as those of supreme excellence;
second, from "Sudhana sees Samantabhadra" onwards, the vision of the functioning of the dharmadhātu.
3. From "Samantabhadra then extended his hand" onwards, he causes [the practitioners] to attain samādhi;
4. From "Samantabhadra addressed [them]" onwards, there is an inquiry into the settled matter, which has three parts: first, the question; second, the answer; third, the praise of virtues.
The first section, on the excellence of the text, contains nine meanings; it is equal to that of all Tathāgatas, thus numbering ten.
Second, within the section on the application of views and practices, there are four parts:
the first clarifies external application through transformation.
Second, from "Re-examining Samantabhadra" onwards, there is the internal application of gathering and transforming beings;
third, from "The Ten Directions" onwards, there is the conclusion regarding the realization of equality, which consists of five phrases;
fourth, from "Sudhana sees Samantabhadra" onwards, it clarifies the benefit Sudhana gains through the ten gates of indestructible wisdom.
The initial section has two parts:
first, the explanation of the nineteen functions of arising; second, the conclusion.
Within the second part, there are two sub-sections:
First is the explanation, followed by the conclusion.
Regarding Sudhana’s attainment of benefit, the text has two parts:
first, a general summary of the ten gates; second, a detailed analysis.
Regarding the three parts of obtaining samādhi through the empowerment of the hand-touching (samāpavarta):
first, the touching; second, the attainment of benefit; third, the conclusion and correlation beginning with "In this way.
Within the second section, the benefit from the hand-touching, there are six points which may be understood accordingly.
Within the section on "Exhorting to Practice the Primordial Supreme Conduct," there are seven parts:
first, attaining the power and function of supreme mastery by virtue of having long cultivated the bodhicitta;
second, [the passage beginning with] "That which I have practiced" and below, illustrating that the virtues are inexhaustible.
3. From "I have attained such [a state]" onwards, he cites what has already been attained to exhort practice;
4. From "You should first observe" onwards, he exhorts the observation of present phenomena, which can be understood as having three phrases;
5. From "If there are sentient beings who hear my name" onwards, he reveals the profound and vast nature of his virtues, which consists of five phrases.
Six: From "Hearing and Cultivating" onwards, it clarifies that the great mind and great practices should likewise give rise to [realization]; this section contains two phrases.
Seven: From "You should further observe me" onwards, it exhorts the observation of the great function of the three bodies.
Those who were born into the pure worlds during the sixth stage previously were born into the *saṃbhogakāya* lands.

Those who are born within my pure body are born into the *dharmakāya* alone; as the text says: "The physical marks of Samantabhadra are like empty space; he relies upon suchness (*tathatā*), not upon buddha-lands."
The seventh section has two parts:
first, exhortation; second, contemplation, which fully reveals cause and effect.
Third, the evaluation of conduct and virtue, which has three parts:
First, the explicit clarification of the examination;
second, the explanation and establishment [of that point] by means of the phrase "For what reason," which may be understood to have three parts;
third, from the passage beginning "He does not vanish from this world," the praise of Sudhana’s inconceivable mastery, revealing its supreme significance.
The fourth section praises the excellence of Sudhana’s practice and consists of two parts:
first, the perfection of the cause; second, the fulfillment of the fruit, beginning with the words "before long.
Within the section on the fruit, the general and the specific aspects can be understood accordingly.
These five verses praise the Buddha.

The reason for praising the Buddha is to clarify that while Samantabhadra Bodhisattva presides before the assembly to receive and guide through his transformative power, it is the Buddha in whom these practices reach their ultimate fulfillment and perfection; therefore, he is praised.
Furthermore, one may praise the power of the causal stage by way of its fruit, which is precisely what is being recounted here.
The verse consists of two parts:
first, the prose introduction, and second, the verse itself.
There are ninety-nine and a half verses, which consist of three parts:
first, the initial eight verses briefly enumerate the merits of the Tathāgata and Bodhisattvas and command the audience to listen and permit the discourse;
second, the subsequent eighty-nine and a half verses specifically praise the transformative functions of the Tathāgata’s three bodies.
The third section has two parts: the exhortation and the practice.
The first part contains three sections:
the first half exhorts [the audience] to listen;
Next, the four and a half verses briefly praise the virtues of the Tathāgata’s three bodies;
the final three verses praise the merits of Samantabhadra, declaring that what has been taught is not in vain and exhorting beings to give rise to faith.

Within the first three bodies, the first half [of the verses] praises the merit of the cessation of the *dharmakāya*; the next one praises the wisdom-merit of the *saṃbhogakāya*; and the following two praise the grace-merit of the *nirmāṇakāya*.
In the second section, the extensive praise, there are three parts:

first, twenty and a half verses praise the merit of the *saṃbhogakāya*; second, from "Sometimes he is seen as Śākyamuni" onwards, sixty-three verses praise the merit of the *nirmāṇakāya*; and third, from "The Tathāgata’s pure *dharmakāya*" onwards, six stanzas praise the merit of the *dharmakāya*.
Question:
Why is it that at the conclusion of the reiteration, one praises the virtues of the Buddha? Answer:
This is the "Explanatory Elucidation," because it establishes the limits of the cause by citing its fruit.
The remainder may be inferred accordingly.
Within the *saṃbhogakāya* (recompense body), there are five [aspects]:
First, the initial three [verses] praise the skillfulness in the two types of knowledge—reasoning and scriptural authority;

second, the four [verses] beginning with "Or seeing the Tathāgata sitting" clarify that his virtue is universally pervasive, being the domain of the great mind alone and not an object of small wisdom;
third, the seven [verses] beginning with "Or seeing Vairocana" clarify that the virtues of all Buddhas equally possess the dharmakāya, the pure land, and the supreme retinue.
4. From "Or one may see a single pore" through the next five and a half lines, there is an analysis of the great function that is without spatial direction;
5. From "In this way" onwards, the conclusion states that it is difficult to exhaustively describe.
Within the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), there are three [sections]:
The first twenty and a half verses praise the great function of the Buddha’s bodily karma;

next, the twenty-two verses from "Abiding in the Unsurpassed Path" onwards praise the Buddha’s oral karma of teaching and transforming; and finally, the twenty and a half verses from "The Buddhas, the Honored Teachers and Guides" onwards praise the Buddha’s mental karma of skillful gathering and benefiting.
The first body has four aspects:

first, one is the transformation of Śākyamuni’s body; second, seven are the manifestations of various causal practices and the transformation of attaining enlightenment through the eight phases; third, five are the manifestations of other Buddhas ascending to heaven and so forth; and fourth, seven and a half are the capacities to manifest various benefits according to conditions, such as bestowing predictions of enlightenment.
There are three sections within the "Oral" [chapter]:

first, five verses clarify that the Dharma taught possesses great majestic power; second, twelve verses clarify how a single voice accords with capacities to respond to karmic conditions; third, five verses distinguish the reasons for the realization of virtuous functions.
Within the preceding twelve [verses], the first four clarify how a single sound is heard differently according to the listener; the subsequent eight summarize the distinctions among the teachings.
Within this section, there are two parts:
first, the twelve [verses] praise the skillfulness of its application; second, from "For example" onwards, eight and a half verses use metaphors to reveal it.

There are five distinct metaphors: first, the metaphor of accomplishing according to benefit; second, the metaphor of appearing in the mind within objects; third, the metaphor of appearing in accordance with images; fourth, the metaphor of generating and protecting; and fifth, the metaphor of generating virtues in objects. These five constitute the great net for gathering and transforming beings.
The remainder of the text may be understood accordingly.
Within the six verses on the *dharmakāya*, there are three parts:

first, one half-verse praises the *dharmakāya* as possessing five characteristics; second, from "Just as what is seen in a dream" onwards, it generally clarifies the meaning through analogies; third, two verses provide the application to the Dharma (*dharmasaṃprayoga*).
The illustrative text consists of two parts:
the first half establishes [the point] by means of principle, while the second part clarifies the Dharma by means of phenomena.

Regarding the five characteristics in the first section: the first phrase is the characteristic of purity; the next two phrases are the characteristic of inconceivability; the third is the characteristic of being devoid of both the conditioned and the unconditioned; and the fourth phrase is the characteristic of being untainted.
Regarding the sixth point, "reaching everywhere without moving," this is characterized by the fifth [point], "eternal abiding.
In the subsequent two sections on the summary and exhortation, the first raises four metaphors to illustrate that his virtues are inexhaustible.

The fourth consists of four analogies: first, the analogy of the boundlessness of the awakened mind; second, the analogy of the inexhaustibility of phenomena; third, the analogy of the profound, vast, and great number; and fourth, the analogy of the limitless expanse of space.
This can be understood through inference; it simply means that the Buddha’s virtues are profound and far-reaching.
Next, a single passage is cited to encourage practice, which constitutes the *Pravartana-bhāga* (the section on dissemination).
This sutra originally consisted of one hundred thousand verses, whereas this commentary contains only thirty-six thousand verses; the meaning of the remaining portion can be inferred.
